note: An outer fortification protecting a gate or bridge: a defensive entrance before the main entrance.
short: An outer fortification guarding an entrance.

note: A ruler with absolute power.
short: An absolute ruler.

note: A concealed dungeon entered through an opening above. The French name is related to forgetting.
short: A dungeon entered through a trapdoor above.

note: Ritual practice intended to call upon or work through divine powers.
short: Ritual practice invoking divine powers.

note: A large burial ground or cemetery; literally a city of the dead.
short: A large cemetery; a city of the dead.

note: One of the solid upright sections of a battlement, between the gaps.
short: A solid upright section of a battlement.

note: A lightly equipped ancient Greek infantryman, named for the small shield carried.
short: A lightly armed ancient Greek infantryman.

note: Green or blue-green corrosion products on copper and its alloys; also a historical pigment name.
short: Greenish corrosion on copper or its alloys.

note: A three-armed emblem, usually formed from three bent legs or three spirals radiating from one center. Also called a triskelion.
short: A three-armed emblem of legs or spirals.

note: A person who eats raw meat.
short: Someone who eats raw meat.

note: The personification of primordial darkness in Greek mythology. In Hesiod’s Theogony, Erebus emerges from Chaos and, with Night, becomes the parent of Aether and Day.
short: Primordial darkness personified in Greek myth.

note: A monstrous adversary of Zeus in Greek mythology, also called Typhoeus. Hesiod describes him as a son of Earth and Tartarus with a hundred serpent heads. Zeus defeats him with thunderbolts.
short: A many-headed monster opposed to Zeus.

note: An old French-derived form of address meaning lord or sir.
short: An old form of address: lord or sir.

note: An ancient measure based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.
short: An old measure based on the forearm.

note: Uncreated; existing without having been made.
short: Uncreated; existing without having been made.

note: An officer commanding a small division of an ancient Greek army.
short: A commander of an ancient Greek military unit.

note: A spar projecting forward from a ship’s bow, supporting its forward sails and rigging.
short: A spar projecting from a ship’s bow.

note: Behind a ship, or toward its stern.
short: Behind a ship; toward its stern.

note: A rope used to hoist or lower a sail, flag, or spar.
short: A rope used to raise a sail or flag.

note: A sail set on the foremast or toward the forward part of a vessel.
short: A sail on the foremast or forward part of a ship.

note: Stone cut into squared blocks with finished faces for building walls.
short: Squared stone cut for regular masonry.

note: Golden in color or ornamented with gold.
short: Golden or gilded.

note: In a low, quiet voice.
short: In a quiet or lowered voice.

note: Foam or froth, especially on rough water.
short: Foam or froth.

note: The vertical distance between a ship’s waterline and the edge of its upper deck.
short: The height of a ship’s deck above its waterline.

note: A rope or cable supporting a mast from behind.
short: A rope supporting a mast from behind.

note: To flash, sparkle, or give off small bursts of light.
short: To sparkle or flash.

note: Carved; an old form of the word.
short: Carved.

note: Possibly Saint Eata, a seventh-century Northumbrian monk, pupil of Aidan, abbot of Melrose, and bishop of Lindisfarne and Hexham.
short: Possibly Saint Eata, a Northumbrian bishop.

note: Possibly Saint Gurloës, also called Urlo, the first abbot of Sainte-Croix at Quimperlé in Brittany. He died in 1057.
short: Possibly Saint Gurloës, the abbot of Quimperlé.

note: Gjöll, the river on the road to Hel in Norse mythology. Its bridge, Gjallarbrú, is guarded by Móðguðr. Hermóðr crosses it when he journeys to the dead to seek Baldr.
short: Gjöll, the Norse river on the road to Hel.

note: A centaur and ferryman in Greek mythology. Heracles shot him after he attacked Deianira. Before dying, Nessus persuaded her that his blood was a love charm; the poisoned garment she later sent Heracles caused his death.
short: A centaur and ferryman of Greek mythology.

note: French for “moon,” from Latin luna.
short: French for moon.

note: A sword dancer dressed in an elaborate or fantastic costume.
short: A sword dancer in elaborate costume.

note: Possibly Saint Droctoveus, a sixth-century monk and abbot of the Paris monastery later called Saint-Germain-des-Prés. A pupil of Germanus, he is traditionally said to have died around 580.
short: Possibly Droctoveus, a sixth-century abbot in Paris.
An oracle’s shrine.
note: Greek manteion: an oracle, or the sanctuary where a diviner gives an oracular response. The word belongs to the family of mantis, a seer.

short: A wrestling school or exercise court.
note: A palaestra was a place for wrestling and athletic training in ancient Greece or Rome. The Latin word comes from Greek palaistra, related to palē, wrestling. By extension the word can name a school or place of instruction.

short: Possibly Greek: father.
note: Possibly Greek patéra, a form of patéras, father; patéras can also denote a priest.

short: Possibly Greek: mother.
note: Possibly Greek mētéra, mother.

short: A priest who interprets omens.
note: A diviner, especially an official religious interpreter of signs in ancient Rome. Augury sought indications of divine approval or disapproval before an undertaking.

short: A woman credited with prophetic powers.
note: A prophetess through whom a god was believed to speak. Ancient traditions placed sibyls in several regions, including Greece and Italy; the Cumaean Sibyl was especially celebrated.

short: Alchemical mercury or a universal remedy.
note: An old alchemical term for mercury, or for a universal remedy.

short: A religious community’s dwelling.
note: A monastery or convent where members live in community, rather than as solitary hermits. The name ultimately combines Greek words for common and life.

short: An assistant, especially to a bishop.
note: A helper or colleague in an office. In church usage, a coadjutor assists a bishop and may hold the right to succeed that bishop.

short: A presiding officer or spokesman.
note: A person appointed to speak for others, or to preside over an assembly. In ecclesiastical usage the title belongs to the chair of a convocation.

short: A principal clerk.
note: The chief clerk of certain courts or other official bodies. The title derives from words meaning first and notary.

short: Greek “all” or “whole.”
note: Pas is the masculine singular of the Greek word for all or whole. Its corresponding feminine and neuter forms are pasa and pan.

short: Greek “hawk” or “falcon.”
note: Hierax is an ancient Greek word for a hawk or falcon. Its stem hierak- appears in compounds and related names.

short: A many-headed sea monster of Greek myth.
note: A monster inhabiting the rocks opposite Charybdis. In Homer’s Odyssey she has six heads on long necks and snatches sailors from vessels passing her cave.

short: The abyss beneath the underworld.
note: Tartarus, the deep pit below the realm of the dead in Greek cosmology, also personified as a primordial being. In Hesiod the defeated Titans are confined there.

short: A Siren whose name means “song.”
note: Molpe is one of the Sirens named in the Hesiodic tradition. The Sirens’ alluring song draws passing sailors toward destruction. Her Greek name means song.

short: One of the Sirens of Greek tradition.
note: A Siren named in the account attributed to Apollodorus. The Sirens are supernatural singers whose voices enchant those who hear them.

short: The Greek sphinx.
note: A form of the Greek name for the sphinx: a creature with a lion’s body, a woman’s head, and wings. The Theban sphinx destroyed travelers who could not answer her riddle, until Oedipus solved it.

short: Possibly Talos, the bronze guardian of Crete.
note: Possibly Talos, the bronze giant who guarded Crete in Greek myth. In English, talus also means the ankle bone or a slope of accumulated rock fragments.

short: Irish “wing.”
note: Irish sciathán means a wing; it can also denote a projecting side or extension. Its ending is diminutive.

short: A tassel-flowered plant; also fuzzy yarn.
note: Acalypha hispida, a plant with long, furry-looking clusters of red flowers. Chenille also means a fuzzy yarn or fabric; the French word means caterpillar.

short: A Saharan antelope with spiral horns.
note: A pale-coated desert antelope, Addax nasomaculatus, with long, twisted horns. It is native to the Sahara.

short: A northern diving seabird.
note: A short-necked seabird of the family Alcidae, typically black and white. Auks use their wings underwater while diving; the extinct great auk, unlike living auks, was flightless.

short: A bushbaby.
note: A galago, or bushbaby, is a small African primate active chiefly at night and at home in trees. Galagos have large eyes and belong to the family Galagidae. The name is used both broadly and as a zoological genus name.

short: A grass-eating Ethiopian monkey.
note: Theropithecus gelada, a large, long-haired monkey resembling a baboon. It is native to Ethiopia and feeds chiefly on grasses.

short: The anvil-shaped bone of the middle ear.
note: The middle one of the three auditory ossicles, between the malleus and stapes. Its Latin name means anvil, describing its shape.

short: A brilliant Central American trogon.
note: A forest bird with iridescent green upperparts and red underparts. In the resplendent quetzal, the male’s exceptionally long upper tail-coverts extend well beyond the tail itself.

short: A fish with a suction disk on its head.
note: A suckerfish that attaches itself to larger marine animals or other surfaces. The Latin name means delay, from an ancient belief that these fish could hold back a ship.

short: A slow-moving nocturnal primate.
note: A tailless or short-tailed, tree-dwelling primate native to southern Asia. Lorises have large eyes and move deliberately along branches.

short: A nocturnal African tree-dwelling primate.
note: A woolly-coated primate of tropical Africa, with a short tail and a reduced index finger. Pottos move slowly and grip branches firmly.

short: A small, very large-eyed nocturnal primate.
note: A primate of Southeast Asian islands with long hind limbs and a slender tail. Its conspicuously large eyes suit its nocturnal life.

short: A long-legged jumping desert rodent.
note: A small nocturnal rodent of arid parts of Africa and Asia. Its elongated hind legs and long balancing tail support rapid, kangaroo-like leaps.

short: A coarse, naturally brownish wild silk.
note: Silk produced by certain moths other than the domesticated mulberry silkworm. The word, from Hindi and Urdu tasar, also names the moth or caterpillar producing it.

short: Italian “enchantment” or “spell.”
note: Italian incanto means an enchantment, a spell, or the feeling of being charmed. It comes from the word family of incantare, to bewitch by chanting. An identically spelled auction term has a different history.

short: Italian: illustrious or renowned.
note: Italian inclito means renowned, illustrious, or glorious. It is a literary adjective descended from Latin inclutus.

short: The wolverine’s genus.
note: Gulo is the zoological genus containing the wolverine. The Latin word gulo means a glutton.

short: The swordfish’s genus.
note: Xiphias is the genus of the common swordfish. The Greek name is related to xiphos, a sword.

short: The aurochs, an extinct wild ox.
note: An old name for the aurochs, the wild ancestor of domestic cattle. Urus was the Latin name for this animal.

short: A venomous Asian snake.
note: A krait is a venomous Asian snake of the genus Bungarus. Kraits belong to the cobra family, Elapidae; several species are strikingly banded. The English name comes from Hindi.

short: A dry crust of dead tissue.
note: An eschar is a crust of dead tissue left by a burn or other injury. The word comes through Latin from Greek eschara.

short: A greenish magnesium–iron silicate.
note: Olivine is a group of magnesium–iron silicate minerals, commonly olive-green. Transparent material of gem quality is called peridot.

short: Seaweed, especially cast up on shore.
note: Sea wrack is marine vegetation washed onto a beach. Wrack is an old word for seaweed and other material left along the tide line.

short: A large Arctic falcon.
note: Falco rusticolus, the largest species of falcon. Its plumage ranges from dark gray to predominantly white.

short: Italian “cousin.”
note: A cousin: the child of an aunt or uncle. The feminine form is cugina.

short: Italian “leather.”
note: Animal hide prepared by tanning. Italian distinguishes this material word from the living skin.

short: Italian “a group of ten.”
note: A set of ten things or persons; also an approximate quantity of ten. It is formed from dieci, ten.

short: Italian “broad bean.”
note: The broad bean, Vicia faba, or one of its large edible seeds. The Italian name descends from Latin faba.

short: An old Italian coin.
note: A small monetary denomination used in several Italian states; later a familiar word for a small amount of money. The name descends from Latin solidus.

short: Italian “elm.”
note: An elm tree, of the genus Ulmus. The word descends from Latin ulmus.

short: Italian “inside.”
note: Inside or within; an adverb referring to an interior position or movement into an interior.

short: Italian “echo.”
note: An echo: sound heard again after reflection from a surface. The word comes from the Greek name Echo.

short: Dutch “village.”
note: A village or small settlement. Dorp is the ordinary Dutch noun, with the plural dorpen.

short: Dutch “pointer” or “clock hand.”
note: A pointer or indicator, such as the hand of a clock. The noun is formed from wijzen, to point or indicate.

short: Dutch “profession” or “occupation.”
note: A person’s profession, occupation, or calling. The Dutch word is related to the verb beroepen.

short: Dutch “language.”
note: Language or speech; a particular language. Its Dutch plural is talen.

short: Dutch “weapon.”
note: A weapon or arm. The Dutch plural wapens can refer collectively to armaments.

short: Dutch “army.”
note: The Dutch word for an army. A legerman is literally an army-man.

short: Hindi “village.”
note: A village; the Hindi word गाँव is commonly transliterated gā̃v or gaon. Its vowel is nasalized.

short: Hindi “river.”
note: Nadī is the Hindi word for a river, inherited from Sanskrit.

short: Sanskrit “king.”
note: Rājan is a Sanskrit word for a king or ruler. Its nominative singular form rājā is the source of the familiar title raja.

short: Esperanto “the color white.”
note: The Esperanto noun for the color white. The corresponding adjective is blanka.

short: Possibly Dutch azijn: vinegar.
note: Possibly Dutch azijn, vinegar.

short: A fleshy-leaved stonecrop.
note: Hylotelephium telephium, formerly Sedum telephium, is a perennial succulent with clusters of small, star-shaped pink or purplish flowers. It is also called live-forever.

short: An aromatic herb with yellow flower buttons.
note: Tanacetum vulgare has finely divided, fernlike leaves and dense clusters of yellow flowers. The crushed foliage has a strong, camphorlike scent.

short: Hebrew “raven.”
note: The Hebrew noun orev means a raven or crow. The older transliteration Oreb preserves a b for the same Hebrew consonant.

short: An ancient name of Aphrodite.
note: Kypris, also written Cypris, is a name of Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love and beauty.

short: A half-woman, half-serpent of Greek myth.
note: In Hesiod’s Theogony, Echidna has a nymph’s upper body and an immense snake’s lower body. With Typhon she is the mother of monsters including Cerberus and the Hydra.

short: A visible appearance of a deity.
note: A manifestation in which a god becomes visible. The word comes through Greek theophaneia, combining the divine with the idea of appearing.

short: Spanish “municipal council.”
note: The governing council of a town or city, consisting of its mayor and councillors.

short: Spanish “court of law.”
note: A court or judicial office; also the place where the judge exercises that office.

short: Spanish “shore” or “bank.”
note: The edge of a body of water: the shore of the sea, or the bank of a river or lake.

short: A tree-lined walk or avenue.
note: Spanish alameda originally denotes a grove of poplars; it also names a public walk planted with trees.

short: A bristly-headed plant used in cloth finishing.
note: A plant of the genus Dipsacus. The dried heads of fuller’s teasel have hooked prickles and were used to raise a nap on woven cloth.

short: A genus of molds with rounded spore cases.
note: Mucor is a genus of molds that form fluffy colonies and produce spores in rounded spore cases at the tips of upright stalks.

short: An earthball fungus.
note: Scleroderma is a genus of tough-skinned, puffball-like fungi. Their interior darkens as the spores mature; the fungi form close associations with tree roots.

short: A glossy black, red-legged crow relative.
note: A bird of the genus Pyrrhocorax, with dark, glossy plumage and red legs. The English name is pronounced “chuff.”

short: Latin “marshy places.”
note: Palustria is a neuter plural form of the Latin adjective paluster, marshy or swampy. It belongs to the same word family as palus, a marsh.

short: Latin “city.”
note: A city or walled town. In Roman usage, urbs without further qualification can mean Rome itself.

short: Greek “pig” or “swine.”
note: Ancient Greek hus, written ὗς, means a pig or hog. The noun can be used of either sex.

short: An earthy deposit rich in lime.
note: Loose or crumbly sediment containing a substantial amount of calcium carbonate, mixed with materials such as clay, sand, or silt.

short: A metal used to strengthen steel.
note: A metallic element, symbol Mo, added to steel for strength and hardness. Its name descends from Greek molybdos, lead.

short: A tropical tree with tart fruit pods.
note: Tamarindus indica produces brown pods containing sticky, acidic pulp around its seeds. The name comes from an Arabic expression meaning Indian date.

short: A dog.
note: An old cant word for a dog, recorded in Francis Grose’s dictionary of slang.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: Food or provisions.
note: Food carried or obtained for a meal. As a verb, prog also means to forage.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: A woman.
note: An old cant term for a woman, as recorded in Grose’s historical slang dictionary.

sources.label: Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: Possibly Latin fuligo: soot.
note: Possibly Latin fuligo, soot. The related English adjective fuliginous means sooty or dark and smoky.

short: Possibly Máel Ruba of Applecross.
note: Possibly Máel Ruba, the Irish-born founder of Applecross in western Scotland in 673. Malrubius is a recorded Latinized form of his name. Later traditions present him as a martyr killed by Norse raiders, but their places and dates are not consistent with the early annalistic record.

short: Possibly an early Egyptian hermit.
note: Possibly Palaemon, the Egyptian hermit who instructed Saint Pachomius in ascetic life. Pachomius later established organized monastic communities; Palaemon represents the older discipline of the solitary desert monk.

short: Possibly Saint Roch, a pilgrim and healer.
note: Possibly Saint Roch, the French pilgrim traditionally invoked against plague. His legend describes his care for sick people in Italy, his own illness, and a dog bringing him bread. French roche also means rock.

short: Shining with brilliant light.
note: Brightly shining or radiant, especially with reflected or splendid light. It is a more emphatic word than merely visible or pale.

short: Dutch: hammer.
note: Dutch hamer means a hammer. It belongs to the same Germanic word family as English hammer.

short: Dutch: an expert or connoisseur.
note: Dutch kenner is someone who knows a subject well: an expert, judge, or connoisseur. It comes from kennen, to know or be acquainted with.

short: Dutch: pearl.
note: Dutch parel means a pearl. Like English pearl, it also admits a figurative sense of something precious or exceptionally fine.

short: Dutch: a numeral, digit, or school grade.
note: Dutch cijfer means a numeral or digit; it can also mean a mark or grade awarded for schoolwork.

short: Dutch: sluggish or indolent.
note: Dutch vadsig means sluggish, indolent, or flabby.

short: Dutch: quick or agile.
note: Dutch vlug means quick, nimble, or agile. It can describe speed in movement or in doing a task.

short: Dutch: heavy.
note: Dutch zwaar means heavy, and extends to something weighty, severe, or difficult. The basic image is a burden with substantial weight.

short: Dutch: danger or peril.
note: Dutch gevaar means danger or peril. The related adjective gevaarlijk means dangerous.

short: Dutch: lion.
note: Dutch leeuw means a lion. The plural is leeuwen; the feminine leeuwin means a lioness.

short: Dutch: wet.
note: Dutch nat means wet. As a noun, it can also mean moisture or liquid.

short: Dutch: large city.
note: A joining of Dutch grote, “large” or “great,” and stad, “city” or “town.” The compound can therefore be read as “large city.”

short: Dutch: knowable or recognizable.
note: Dutch kenbaar means knowable, recognizable, or capable of being made known. The suffix -baar is comparable to English -able.

short: Possibly Dutch aanvegen: to sweep up.
note: Possibly Dutch aanvegen, to sweep up or sweep a place clean.

short: Italian: honorific or honorary.
note: The feminine form of Italian onorifico: conferring honor, or honorary rather than carrying the full duties or material advantages of an office.

short: Italian: luxuriant growth or vigor.
note: Italian rigoglio names vigorous, flourishing growth, especially of plants. It also extends to bodily vigor, fullness, or exuberance.

short: Italian: a reply or cross-reference.
note: Italian rimando can mean a reply, return, or cross-reference. A rarer sense is postponement or deferral, so the associated idea of delay is also linguistically possible.

short: Italian: a payment or disbursement.
note: Italian sborso is the act of paying money out, or the sum paid. It is related to sborsare, to disburse, with the image of money coming out of a purse.

short: Italian: cackles or makes a racket.
note: A form of Italian schiamazzare: to cackle, squawk, or make a noisy commotion. The verb is used of poultry and other birds, and by extension of noisy people.

short: Italian: a fur cap.
note: Italian colbacco is a fur cap, especially a tall military one, though the word also covers civilian fur hats. Its history runs through French colback to Turkish kalpak.

short: Italian: vigorous or robust.
note: Italian gagliardo means strong, robust, or full of vigor. It can describe a person, a forceful action, or something potent such as wind or strong wine.

short: Italian: joyful.
note: Italian gioioso means joyful or full of delight. It is formed from gioia, joy.

short: Italian: suitable or fitted.
note: The feminine form of Italian adatto: suitable, fitted, or well adapted to a purpose. Of a person, it can imply an aptitude for a task.

short: Italian: a black horse or its coloring.
note: Italian morello describes a black or nearly black color, especially a horse’s coat. Used as a noun, it can mean a black horse.

short: Italian: a blackberry or mulberry.
note: Italian mora is the fruit of a bramble or mulberry tree. Both can be dark, clustered fruits, though a blackberry and a mulberry are botanically different structures.

short: Italian: a small pot or jug.
note: Italian bricco is a small vessel with a pouring spout, traditionally made of metal and used for coffee or boiling milk.

short: Italian: helmet.
note: Italian casco means a helmet or protective head covering. It is related to Spanish casco, a shell or helmet.

short: Italian: hand.
note: Italian mano means a hand. It continues Latin manus and is grammatically feminine, despite ending in -o; its usual plural is mani.

short: Italian: face or countenance.
note: Italian volto means the face or countenance. It can include the expression or aspect presented by a face, rather than just its physical surface.

short: Italian: skilled; an expert.
note: Italian perito means skilled or experienced; as a noun, an expert or specialist. It is related to Latin peritus, experienced.

short: Italian: third.
note: Italian terzo means third, the ordinal following second. It can also stand for a third part or a third person in a group.

short: Italian: a little beetle or cockroach.
note: Italian bacherozzolo names a small dark beetle, especially a darkling beetle, and is also used popularly for a cockroach or similar insect. The diminutive belongs to the family of baco, a worm or grub.

short: Possibly Italian affitto: rent, lease, or hire.
note: Possibly Italian affitto, rent, lease, or hire.

short: Italian: large city.
note: A joining of Italian grande, “large” or “great,” and città, “city.” Città descends from Latin civitas, originally the community or body of citizens.

short: Italian: new city.
note: Italian novella città can be read as “new city”: novella is a feminine form of novello, new or young. The final accent in ordinary Italian città marks the stressed last syllable.

short: Hindi: firefly.
note: Hindi jugnū, also jugunū, means a firefly or glow-worm. The word names a light-bearing insect; the spelling Juganu approximates one of its spoken forms.

short: Hindi: pearl.
note: Hindi motī means a pearl. It is different from moṭā, “fat” or “thick”: the vowels and the kind of t distinguish the words.

short: Hindi: thick or stout.
note: Hindi moṭā means thick, stout, or broad. The retroflex ṭ is made with the tongue turned back; ordinary English transliteration usually leaves that distinction unmarked.

short: Hindi and Urdu: guest.
note: Hindi and Urdu mehmān mean a guest. The word was borrowed from Persian and retains the sense of someone received with hospitality.

short: Hindi and Urdu: salt.
note: Hindi and Urdu namak mean salt. The word was borrowed from Persian.

short: Hindi: red.
note: Hindi lāl means red, as a color or adjective.

short: Hindi: first.
note: Hindi pahlā, often written pehla in English, is the ordinal first. Its ordinary feminine form is pahlī.

short: Hindi: small or younger.
note: Hindi choṭā means small or little. It also expresses relative age or rank: younger, junior, or lesser, not only physical size.

short: Hindi and Urdu: plum.
note: Hindi and Urdu ālūbukhārā mean a plum. The name comes through Persian and contains Bukhara, the Central Asian city, rather than the separate modern Hindi word for a potato.

short: Hindi: rain or the rainy season.
note: Hindi barsāt means rain, rainfall, or the rainy season. It belongs to the word family concerned with raining.

short: Hindi: an elephant keeper or driver.
note: Hindi mahāvat means an elephant keeper or driver, the occupation known in English as a mahout.

short: Possibly Hindi: false or counterfeit.
note: Possibly Hindi jālī, “false,” “forged,” or “counterfeit,” an adjective borrowed through Persian. A separate Hindi jālī means a net or lattice. The identical English-looking spelling conceals two different word histories.

short: Possibly Hindi: silver.
note: Possibly Hindi cā̃dī, usually written chandi in English, meaning silver. The nasalized vowel is often left unmarked in transliteration; a similarly romanized divine name has different consonants and vowels.

short: Malay: tiger.
note: Malay and Indonesian harimau mean tiger. The two-word spelling Hari Mau separates the syllables into a name-like pair.

short: Possibly Old French: a circle.
note: Possibly Old French viron, a circle or the country round about. It belongs to the family of virer, “to turn,” and environ, “around.”

short: Possibly Termagant, a medieval stage deity.
note: Possibly Termagant, an imaginary deity of medieval European literature. Christian writers wrongly ascribed this figure to Muslims; on the stage the character became a noisy, overbearing tyrant. The later English insult termagant developed from that theatrical tradition.

short: Spanish: a protective wire screen.
note: Spanish alambrera is wire mesh or a protective wire cover, such as a screen over a window or food. It is formed from alambre, wire; the central image is an enclosing barrier.

short: A walrus’s penile bone.
note: An oosik is the baculum, or penile bone, of a walrus. The word comes from Iñupiaq usuk. It names a particular anatomical structure, not the animal as a whole.

short: Possibly Gaelic: the mountains.
note: Possibly Scottish Gaelic na beanntan, the mountains. Beanntan is the plural of beinn, a mountain or peak.

short: German: vulture.
note: German Geier means a vulture.

short: Polish: rifle.
note: Polish karabin is a rifle or other long firearm. It belongs to the international word family of carbine, but in Polish it is not restricted to a short cavalry weapon.

short: German: scepter.
note: German Zepter is a scepter, the staff carried as an emblem of authority. The word ultimately comes from Greek skēptron, a staff.

short: Serbo-Croatian: bitter.
note: Serbo-Croatian gorak means bitter. Its basic sense concerns taste; it also permits the familiar figurative sense of a painful or disagreeable experience.

short: Serbo-Croatian: cabbage.
note: Serbo-Croatian kupus means cabbage, the leafy vegetable. The spelling is an ordinary noun used as a name.

short: Latin: a school or place of study.
note: Latin schola means a school, lecture, or learned discussion. It comes from Greek scholē, leisure devoted to study: the word’s history links learning with time free from other work.

short: Possibly Greek chrēsmos, an oracle or prophetic response.
note: Possibly Greek chrēsmos, an oracle or prophetic response, often delivered in verse.

short: A stand or frame for a coffin.
note: A frame or stand on which a dead body or coffin is carried or displayed. The word is related to bear in the sense of carrying a weight.

short: A railing supported by small pillars.
note: A row of small pillars, called balusters, supporting a rail. The term names the whole barrier along a stair, balcony, or terrace, rather than one of its supports.

short: A small lake, especially in the hills.
note: A small lake, especially one in mountainous country. The word came into English from Old Norse and remains common in the place-names of northern Britain.

short: Italian: a witch.
note: Italian strega means a witch. The word descends from Latin striga, related to strix, a night bird associated in ancient belief with uncanny or harmful powers.

short: A dervish: a religious ascetic.
note: An older spelling of dervish, a member of a Muslim religious order associated with ascetic devotion. The word comes from Persian darvish, originally a poor person or beggar; it is broader than the particular order known for whirling ceremonies.

short: Silkworm fiber.
note: The fine fiber spun by silkworms and used to make cloth. The word also denotes the threadlike styles of an ear of corn.

short: A plant with stinging hairs.
note: A plant, especially of the genus Urtica, bearing hairs that sting the skin. As a verb, nettle means to irritate or provoke.

short: A fragrant bulb; also a name with a Greek flower myth.
note: A fragrant bulbous plant, especially Hyacinthus orientalis; also an old gemstone name. In Greek myth, Apollo’s beloved Hyacinthus died after a discus struck him, and a flower grew from his blood.

short: A polishable metamorphic rock.
note: Limestone transformed by heat and pressure into crystalline rock, widely used for sculpture and buildings.

short: A predatory freshwater fish.
note: A long-bodied freshwater fish with prominent teeth. Pike also denotes a long thrusting spear.

short: An animal scent used in perfumery.
note: A strongly scented secretion of the male musk deer; also similar fragrances and their substitutes.

short: An aromatic herb with a Greek transformation myth.
note: An aromatic herb of the genus Mentha, including peppermint and spearmint. In Greek myth, the nymph Menthe was transformed by Persephone into fragrant mint.

short: A flowering shrub of the genus Rosa.
note: A shrub of the genus Rosa, or its flower, commonly bearing prickles and fragrant blossoms.

short: A tendon; figuratively, strength.
note: A tendon: the tough tissue joining muscle to bone. Figuratively, bodily strength or a source of strength.

short: A counted gathering of paper.
note: A quantity of paper, traditionally twenty-four sheets and in some usages twenty-five. The word’s history also involves sheets folded together. It does not specify a universal number of written pages.

short: Possibly Greek: a lake or pool.
note: Possibly Greek límnē, a lake, pool, or marsh.

short: Possibly Spanish alcalde: mayor.
note: Possibly Spanish alcalde, a mayor or municipal magistrate, from Arabic al-qāḍī, the judge.

short: A spiral, coil, or ring.
note: A spiral or coil; also an arrangement of leaves, petals, or other parts in a ring around an axis.

short: A stone used as a hammer.
note: A stone used for pounding or striking, especially a prehistoric tool used to shape other stones.

short: A small freshwater fish.
note: A small freshwater fish of the carp family, especially the European Leuciscus leuciscus; the name also applies to several North American fishes.

short: A male cat, especially a castrated one.
note: An old word for a male cat, particularly a castrated male. It originated as a familiar form of the name Gilbert.

short: An evening church service.
note: Evening prayer in Christian worship, especially the sung evening service of the Anglican tradition.

short: The genus of pepper plants.
note: A genus of plants in the nightshade family that includes sweet peppers and chili peppers; also their fruit.

short: Possibly Rome’s Palatine Hill, site of imperial palaces.
note: Possibly the Palatine Hill, one of Rome’s seven hills, where aristocratic houses and later imperial palaces were built. The related adjective palatine means belonging to a palace or possessing royal authority.

short: A queen or a raja’s wife.
note: A queen in South Asia, or the wife of a raja. From Hindi and Urdu rānī, ultimately Sanskrit rājñī.

short: A blackbird.
note: Merl or merle: an old word for the European blackbird.

short: A large American shorebird.
note: A stocky shorebird with long legs, a straight bill, and striking black-and-white wing markings.

short: A plant with conspicuous flower clusters.
note: Blazing star is a common name for several plants, including Liatris, with spikes of purple flowers, and species of Mentzelia. It is also an archaic term for a comet.

short: Dutch: a bow or snare.
note: Dutch strik means a bow tied in ribbon or cord, or a snare for catching animals.

short: Possibly Italian: I challenge.
note: Possibly Italian sfido, I challenge or I defy, from the verb sfidare.

short: Italian: a mountain pass or crossing.
note: Italian valico means a crossing or a pass through a mountain range.

short: Possibly quadrifrons: four-faced.
note: Possibly Latin quadrifrons, four-faced. The term describes a four-fronted Roman arch and occurs in the name Janus Quadrifrons.

short: Possibly Semele’s divine name.
note: Possibly Thyone, the name of Semele after her elevation to divine status in Greek myth. Semele was the mother of Dionysus.

short: Possibly the Crommyonian Sow.
note: Possibly Phaea, the fierce Crommyonian Sow killed by Theseus in Greek myth.

short: Possibly Esperanto: duke.
note: Possibly Esperanto duko, duke, a title of nobility.

short: Italian: beautiful or handsome.
note: Italian bello means beautiful or handsome; its feminine form is bella.

short: Italian: alive, lively, or vivid.
note: Italian vivo means alive or living. It also describes something lively, vivid, or intense.

short: Italian: Turkish, or a Turk.
note: Italian turco means Turkish; as a noun, a Turk or the Turkish language.

short: Italian: silent or quiet.
note: Italian zitta is the feminine form of zitto, silent or quiet. It can be used as an instruction to keep quiet.

short: Italian: March, the month.
note: Italian marzo means March, the month. Its name comes from Latin Martius, associated with Mars.

short: Italian: a body or organized group.
note: Italian corpo means a body, and by extension an organized group or corporate body.

short: Italian: an exit or departure.
note: Italian uscita means an exit, departure, or outing; it is related to uscire, to go out.

short: Possibly Italian urbanità: civility or refined manners.
note: Possibly Italian urbanità, courtesy, civility, or refinement of manners. The word descends from Latin urbanitas, originally the cultivated manners associated with city life.

short: Possibly Italian solenne: solemn or stately.
note: Possibly Italian solenne, solemn, ceremonial, or stately; something marked by seriousness and dignity.

short: Possibly Salic: relating to the laws of the Salian Franks.
note: Possibly Italian salica, the feminine form of salico, Salic. The Lex Salica was the law code of the Salian Franks; one provision excluded women from inheriting certain land.

short: Possibly Italian ugola: the uvula.
note: Possibly Italian ugola, the uvula: the small fleshy projection hanging from the soft palate at the back of the mouth. Its Latin ancestor uvula means little grape.

short: Italian: dark or brown.
note: Italian bruna is the feminine form of bruno, dark or brown, especially of hair or complexion.

short: Possibly Italian attento: attentive or careful.
note: Possibly Italian attento, attentive, careful, or alert. As an exclamation, attento! means watch out.

short: Anglo-Norman: my lord.
note: An attested Anglo-Norman spelling of munsire or messire, a respectful title meaning my lord. The related modern French form is monsieur.

short: Possibly Dutch rechter: a judge.
note: Possibly Dutch rechter, a judge: someone who hears cases and delivers judgments. It is formed from recht, law or justice.

short: Dutch: sick or ill.
note: Dutch ziek means sick or ill.

short: Possibly Italian legare: to bind or tie.
note: Possibly an old Italian form of legare, to bind, tie, or fasten. The verb also describes bonds of marriage, friendship, and obligation.

short: Hindi: a knife.
note: Hindi cākū means a knife, a cutting tool or weapon with a blade attached to a handle.

short: Hindi: Monday.
note: Hindi somvār means Monday.

short: Hindi: ninth.
note: Hindi nauvā̃ means ninth, the ordinal number following eighth.

short: Possibly Hindi bālā: a girl or young woman.
note: Possibly Hindi bālā, a girl or young woman.

short: Possibly shauq: desire or enthusiasm.
note: Possibly Hindi and Urdu shauq, desire, enthusiasm, or a strong interest in something. The word is borrowed from Arabic.

short: Possibly Persian bahār: springtime or flourishing beauty.
note: Possibly Persian bahār, also used in Urdu, meaning springtime, flourishing beauty, or splendor.

short: Possibly Hindi thoṛī: a little or scanty.
note: Possibly Hindi thoṛī, a feminine form meaning a little, scanty, or few.

short: Possibly nādār: poor or without possessions.
note: Possibly Persian and Urdu nādār, poor or without possessions.

short: Possibly Swahili maliki: a ruler or sovereign.
note: Possibly Swahili maliki, a king, ruler, or sovereign, from Arabic. The related malkia means a queen.

short: Swahili: courage or heroism.
note: Swahili ushujaa means bravery, courage, or heroism. It is related to shujaa, a hero or courageous person.

short: Turkish: salt.
note: Turkish tuz means salt.

short: Possibly Ottoman Turkish miralay: colonel.
note: Possibly Ottoman Turkish miralay, a colonel or commander of a regiment.

short: Finnish: alone.
note: Finnish yksin means alone or by oneself.

short: Dutch: an advocate or lawyer.
note: Dutch advocaat means an advocate or lawyer, someone who gives legal advice or represents a party in court.

short: Latin: a sitting room.
note: Latin sellaria means a sitting room or a room furnished with seats. It is formed from sella, a chair or seat.

short: Possibly the pájaro Cú, a bird of Mexican folklore.
note: Possibly the pájaro Cú of Mexican folklore, a bird given borrowed feathers by other birds. In versions of the tale, its disappearance explains why the owl calls for it at night and the roadrunner searches for it.

sources.label: Core Knowledge: Birds Through the Seasons

short: Possibly Saint Flannan of Killaloe.
note: Possibly Saint Flannan, a seventh-century Irish churchman associated with Killaloe. Later traditions remember him as its abbot and bishop; the cathedral there bears his name.

short: Possibly Morpheus, the shaper of human figures in dreams.
note: Possibly Morpheus, the dream spirit in Ovid’s Metamorphoses who can imitate human appearance, movement, and speech. He is a son of Sleep.

short: Possibly Malay teras: heartwood or an essential core.
note: Possibly Malay teras, heartwood, the hard inner part of a tree trunk. Figuratively it means a core, foundation, or essential part.

short: Possibly Swedish torda: a razorbill.
note: Possibly Swedish torda, an old name for the razorbill, Alca torda. This black-and-white seabird is a member of the auk family.

sources.label: A. F. Dalin, Dictionary of the Swedish Language

short: Possibly the Han dynasty of China.
note: Possibly the Han dynasty of China, traditionally dated 206 BCE–220 CE. It is divided into Western and Eastern Han, separated by the brief Xin dynasty.

short: Arabic: a village.
note: Arabic qarya means a village; its plural is qura.

short: Dutch: a fellow or chap.
note: Dutch vent is an informal word for a man, fellow, or chap. Its tone can be dismissive.

short: Possibly Dutch versregel: a line of poetry.
note: Possibly Dutch versregel, a line of verse or poetry.

short: Dutch: rock candy or crystallized sugar.
note: Dutch kandij means crystallized sugar or rock candy. It comes through French candi from Arabic qandī, associated with sugar cane.

short: Possibly Italian volante: a steering wheel.
note: Possibly Italian volante, a steering wheel or handwheel. The related adjective volante means flying.

short: Greek personification of revelry and merrymaking.
note: Comus, or Komos, is the ancient Greek personification of revelry and merrymaking. Philostratus describes him as a drowsy youth attending a drinking party.

short: An Andean camel relative bred for its soft fleece.
note: An alpaca is a South American relative of the camel, domesticated in the Andes for its soft fleece. The two main fleece types are huacaya and suri.

short: A large marine fish of the jack family.
note: Amberjacks are large marine fishes of the jack family. The greater amberjack, Seriola dumerili, has a silvery body with an amber stripe along its side.

short: Another name for a giant anteater or an aardvark.
note: Antbear is another name for the giant anteater of Central and South America. It is also used for the aardvark of Africa.

short: A small tree with pink flowers and heart-shaped leaves.
note: The Judas tree, Cercis siliquastrum, is a small deciduous tree native to southern Europe and western Asia. It bears clusters of rosy-pink, pea-shaped flowers on older wood and has heart-shaped leaves.

short: Possibly Swahili mto: a river.
note: Possibly Swahili mto, a river or stream. Its plural is mito.

short: Possibly Arabic balad: a town or country.
note: Possibly Arabic balad, a town, settlement, district, or country. Its plural is bilād.

sources.label: John Richardson, Persian, Arabic, and English Dictionary

short: Possibly Arabic zahrāʾ: bright or radiant.
note: Possibly Arabic zahrāʾ, shining, bright, or radiant, also used as a woman’s name.

short: Possibly Saint Cilinia, mother of Remigius of Reims.
note: Possibly Saint Cilinia, also called Celinia or Céline, a fifth-century woman of Gaul remembered as the mother of Saint Remigius of Reims.

short: Possibly Saint Tigridia, abbess of Oña.
note: Possibly Saint Tigridia, the first abbess of San Salvador at Oña in northern Spain in the early eleventh century. She was a daughter of the monastery’s founders, Count Sancho García and Urraca.

short: A primrose relative with pale yellow flower clusters.
note: The oxlip, Primula elatior, is a primrose relative with clusters of pale yellow flowers carried above a rosette of leaves.

short: A spring wildflower with drooping yellow flowers.
note: The cowslip, Primula veris, is a spring wildflower with drooping clusters of yellow, cup-shaped flowers. It grows in grassy places, including meadows and open woodland.

short: A fragrant-flowered magnolia; also bay laurel.
note: Sweetbay commonly names Magnolia virginiana, a North American magnolia with fragrant creamy-white flowers. Sweet bay is also a name for Laurus nobilis, the aromatic bay laurel.

short: An evergreen Arbutus tree with peeling bark.
note: A madrone is an evergreen tree of the genus Arbutus. Pacific madrone, Arbutus menziesii, is native to western North America and has reddish-brown bark that peels away from the trunk.

short: A dabbling duck with a white wing patch.
note: The gadwall, Mareca strepera, is a dabbling duck. Males have finely patterned gray-brown plumage; both sexes show a white patch in the wing.

short: An old word for a cricket or a merry person.
note: Grig is an old or dialect word for a cricket or grasshopper. It can also mean a lively, cheerful person, as in the phrase merry as a grig.

short: A stalked crinoid, a marine animal with feathery arms.
note: A sea lily is a stalked crinoid, a marine animal related to sea stars. Its branching, featherlike arms collect food particles from the water.

short: Possibly Esperanto: a Hellene, or Helen.
note: Possibly Esperanto heleno, a Hellene or Greek. Heleno is also used as the Esperanto form of the given name Helen.

short: Possibly Greek polis: a city-state.
note: Possibly Greek polis, a city or city-state: a political community formed around an urban center and its surrounding territory.

sources.label: Thomas R. Martin, Overview of Classical Greek History

short: Possibly Latin urbs and secundus: second city.
note: Possibly a formation from Latin urbs, city, and secundus, second, suggesting second city.

short: Greek: a round shield; also an asp.
note: Greek aspis means a round shield. The same word was also used for the asp, an Egyptian venomous snake.

short: Possibly Sanskrit karṇa: an ear; also the epic hero Karna.
note: Possibly Sanskrit karṇa, an ear. Karna is also the name of Kunti’s son in the Mahābhārata.

short: Possibly Saint Merinus or Merryn, an Irish monastic saint.
note: Possibly Saint Merinus, also called Merryn or Meadhran, an Irish monastic saint remembered as a disciple of Comgall of Bangor and venerated in Ireland and Scotland.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate, The Book of Saints (1921)

note: A mast behind the mainmast, or a fore-and-aft sail carried on that mast; also an adjective for its rigging.
short: A mast behind the mainmast, or its sail.
Possibly Abaia, a great magical eel in Melanesian tradition.
note: Possibly Abaia, a magical eel in a Melanesian flood tale. When people catch fish from its lake, it sends a deluge in retaliation.

short: Possibly the Simurgh, a mythical bird of Iranian tradition.
note: Possibly the Simurgh, or Sēnmurw, the great mythical bird of Iranian tradition. In Persian epic the bird protects Zal and later aids his son Rostam.

short: The entrance vestibule of a church.
note: A vestibule or porch at the entrance of a church, leading into the nave.

short: Latin: a bath or bathing room.
note: Latin balneum means a bath, bathing place, or bathing room. The word was borrowed from Greek balaneion and is the ancestor of English terms beginning balneo-, concerned with baths.

short: Old cant for pretty or fine.
note: Old cant for pretty, fine, or attractive.

sources.label: Grose · Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811)

short: Possibly Saint Mamelta, a Persian martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Mamelta, also called Memelchtha, a fourth-century Persian martyr. Christian tradition describes a priestess of Artemis who converted to Christianity and was stoned.

short: Possibly Arabic siyūf, swords.
note: Possibly Arabic siyūf, swords, a dialectal plural of sayf or sēf, a sword.

sources.label: Willmore, The Spoken Arabic of Egypt (Birzeit University)

short: Possibly Arabic ṣabā, the east wind.
note: Possibly Arabic ṣabā, the east wind; in Arabic and Urdu literary usage, a gentle morning breeze.

short: Possibly Arabic banj, an anesthetic.
note: Possibly Arabic banj, an anesthetic or narcotic; the word also names henbane, a plant historically used for its intoxicating effects.

sources.label: Hans Wehr, A Dictionary of Modern Written Arabic

short: A Madagascan primate; its name derives from Latin spirits of the dead.
note: A primate of Madagascar and nearby islands. Its zoological name derives from Latin lemures, spirits of the dead, originally applied by Linnaeus to animals that wandered at night.

short: A stoat, especially in its white winter coat.
note: A stoat or related weasel whose fur turns white in winter while the tail-tip stays black; also its fur, traditionally used to trim ceremonial robes.

short: Whale skin and attached blubber eaten in Greenland.
note: A Greenlandic food made from whale skin with its attached layer of blubber.

short: Possibly the magical herb in the Odyssey.
note: Possibly the magical herb Hermes gives Odysseus against Circe’s enchantments in the Odyssey. Homer describes a black root and white flowers.

short: A flowering plant whose name is Greek for star.
note: A plant of Aster or related genera, bearing flower heads with radiating petals. The name comes from Greek astēr, star.

short: A flowering plant of the family Orchidaceae.
note: A plant of the family Orchidaceae. Orchid flowers typically have three petals, with one enlarged into a distinctive lip.

short: Latin for a fox.
note: Latin vulpes means a fox; figuratively, cunning or craftiness.

sources.label: Lewis and Short Latin Dictionary, Perseus

short: A predatory songbird that often impales its prey.
note: A bird of the family Laniidae, with a hooked bill. Shrikes often fasten captured insects or other prey onto thorns.

short: Large wild cattle with a shoulder hump.
note: Large wild cattle of the genus Bison, with heavy forequarters, a shoulder hump, and a shaggy coat. Living species are native to North America and Europe.

short: Possibly moor-grass, a tufted grass with purple flower clusters.
note: Possibly moor-grass, especially Molinia caerulea, a tufted perennial grass with narrow leaves and purplish flower clusters.

short: Hindi: a dozen.
note: Hindi darjan means a dozen: a group or quantity of twelve.

short: Hindi: minister of state.
note: Hindi rājya mantrī means minister of state. Rājya means a state or kingdom, and mantrī a minister or counsellor.

sources.label: Government of India: official ministerial titles

short: Possibly a traditional name for a cattle herder.
note: Possibly Kilhari, a name recorded for professional cattle herders in western India. Historical gazetteers associate these herders with breeding oxen.

short: Hindi: bread, especially an unleavened flatbread.
note: Hindi roṭī means bread, especially an unleavened flatbread. The word is also used in English for Indian and Caribbean flatbreads.

short: Possibly Rama, hero of the Ramayana and an incarnation of Vishnu.
note: Possibly Ram or Rama, the hero of the Ramayana and an incarnation of Vishnu in Hindu tradition. Sita is his wife; the epic recounts her abduction and rescue.

short: Japanese: a village.
note: Japanese mura means a village or hamlet. It is also a term for a rural administrative community.

short: German: a joiner or cabinetmaker.
note: German Schreiner means a joiner or cabinetmaker: a craftsperson who makes furniture and other fitted woodwork. It is especially common in southern and western German-speaking regions.

short: Possibly German Flößer: a raftman.
note: Possibly German Flößer, a raftman: someone who guides a raft, traditionally transporting timber down a river.

short: Hindi: the second of August.
note: Hindi dūsrā means second or other; agast is August. Together the words give the date second of August.

sources.label: University of Texas: First Year Hindi

short: Possibly Dutch mevrouw: madam or Mrs.
note: Possibly Dutch mevrouw, a polite title or form of address for a woman, corresponding to Mrs., Ms., or madam.

short: Possibly Italian rimo: I rhyme.
note: Possibly Italian rimo, I rhyme or compose verse, from the verb rimare.

short: Possibly Italian cantore: a singer or chorister.
note: Possibly Italian cantore, a singer, especially a chorister or church singer. The word comes from Latin cantor and can also describe a poet.

short: Possibly Badoura, a princess of the Arabian Nights.
note: Possibly Princess Badoura of the Arabian Nights, a princess of China whose adventures are intertwined with those of Prince Camaralzaman.

short: A straight dagger from the Khyber region.
note: A choora is a straight, single-edged dagger associated with the Khyber region and nearby Pashtun communities. Museum examples have pointed steel blades and shaped horn grips.

short: Scots: watchful or careful.
note: Scots tentie means watchful, attentive, or careful. It is related to tent, heed or attention, as in take tent, take care.

short: Possibly Cocopa skany: to break a long object into pieces.
note: Possibly Cocopa skany, to break a long object into several pieces. Cocopa is a Yuman language spoken in the lower Colorado River region.

sources.label: University of British Columbia: Cocopa Dictionary

short: A stinging jellyfish of the genus Chrysaora.
note: Sea nettles are jellyfish of the genus Chrysaora. Their bells trail long tentacles armed with stinging cells that capture small marine animals.

short: A heat-loving, wingless insect related to silverfish.
note: A firebrat, Thermobia domestica, is a small wingless insect related to silverfish. It thrives in hot places and feeds on starches and other organic material.

short: A small Eurasian diving duck.
note: A smew is a small diving duck, Mergellus albellus, of northern Eurasia. Males are mainly white with black markings; females have reddish-brown heads.

sources.label: Royal Society for the Protection of Birds

short: A northern owl that often hunts by day.
note: The northern hawk owl, Surnia ulula, is a long-tailed owl of northern forests. It hunts largely by day and has a hawk-like silhouette and flight.

short: A flowering shrub of the genus Spiraea.
note: Spireas are deciduous shrubs of the genus Spiraea, in the rose family. Their small flowers grow in conspicuous clusters, often white or pink. The genus name comes from Greek speira, a wreath.

short: A flowering plant also called vervain.
note: Verbena is a genus of flowering plants also called vervains. Their small flowers usually have five lobes and grow in spikes or clusters; many species are cultivated as ornamentals.

short: An aromatic evergreen shrub with white flowers.
note: Common myrtle, Myrtus communis, is an evergreen shrub with aromatic leaves, white flowers, and dark berries. It is native to the Mediterranean region and southwestern Asia.

short: A flowering shrub or vine of the genus Lonicera.
note: Honeysuckles are shrubs or twining climbers of the genus Lonicera. Their tubular or two-lipped flowers are often fragrant and are followed by berries.

short: A small codlike coastal fish.
note: A tomcod is a small codlike fish. The Atlantic tomcod, Microgadus tomcod, lives in coastal waters and estuaries of eastern North America and moves into fresh or brackish water to spawn in winter.

short: Gaelic: brother; braithrean means brothers.
note: Scottish Gaelic bràthair means brother; its plural is bràithrean.

short: Scottish Gaelic: yes or indeed.
note: Scottish Gaelic seadh expresses agreement or acknowledgement: yes, indeed, or uh-huh.

short: An old word for a person; also brave or stalwart.
note: A wight is an old word for a living being, especially a person. A separate archaic adjective, wight, means brave or stalwart.

short: The Greek god of fire and metalworking.
note: Hephaestus is the Greek god of fire and metalworking, the divine smith who fashions weapons and wondrous objects for gods and heroes. His Roman counterpart is Vulcan.

short: A water buffalo.
note: A carabao is a water buffalo. The name entered English through Philippine Spanish from a Visayan word, karabáw.

short: A twilled fabric traditionally made of silk and worsted wool.
note: Bombazine is a twill fabric traditionally woven with silk threads lengthwise and worsted wool crosswise. The name also denotes a black silk twill.

short: Scots words for trouble, bother, or worry.
note: Scots fash means to trouble, annoy, or worry; fashed means troubled or bothered. The verb also occurs as fashes and fashin’, bothering.

short: Scots: ghosts.
note: Scots ghaists means ghosts; the singular is ghaist.

short: Scots: much, large, or great.
note: Scots muckle means much or a great deal, and also large or great in size.

short: Scots: the Devil; also an emphatic exclamation or denial.
note: Scots fient is a form of fiend, especially the Devil. It is used in exclamations and emphatic denials, much like the devil! or not a bit.

short: Scots: fine, splendid, or handsome.
note: Scots braw means fine, splendid, or handsome. It can describe an impressive place, a well-dressed person, or someone strong and good-looking.

short: Possibly Arabic raʾīs: a chief, leader, or captain.
note: Possibly Arabic raʾīs, a chief, leader, or captain, from raʾs, head. The title has also passed into several other languages.

short: A small skin- or fabric-covered boat.
note: A coracle is a small, lightweight boat made from a framework covered with hide or waterproof fabric. The word comes from Welsh corwgl.

short: A metal vessel holding a lighted fire.
note: A cresset is a metal cup or basket that holds burning fuel for illumination, mounted on a pole or hung like a lantern.

short: A small pan or drinking cup.
note: A pannikin is a small pan or drinking cup, especially in British usage. Its name is a diminutive of pan.

short: Rope steps used to climb a ship’s rigging.
note: Ratlines are the short ropes stretched across a sailing ship’s shrouds, forming ladder-like footholds for climbing the rigging.

short: The gaps between a battlement’s raised sections.
note: Crenels are the gaps between the raised sections of a battlement. The raised sections are called merlons.

short: A usually triangular sail set above a gaff.
note: A gaff-topsail is a sail, usually triangular, set above the gaff of a fore-and-aft-rigged vessel. Its lower edge extends along the gaff.

short: Greenish or becoming green.
note: Virescent means greenish or becoming green. It comes from Latin virescere, to grow green.

short: Dark, murky, or gloomy.
note: Tenebrious means dark, murky, or gloomy. It is a form of tenebrous, ultimately from Latin tenebrae, darkness.
